module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 288

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/288](https://www.erdosproblems.com/288)
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace Erdos288

/--
Is it true that there are only finitely many pairs of intervals $I_1$, $I_2$ such that
$$
\sum_{n_1 \in I_1} \frac{1}{n_1} + \sum_{n_2 \in I_2} \frac{1}{n_2} \in \mathbb{N}?
$$
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_288 : answer(sorry) ↔ Set.Finite { I : Fin 2 → ℕ+ × ℕ+ |
    ∀ j, (I j).1 ≤ (I j).2 ∧
      ∃ n : ℕ+, (∑ j : Fin 2, ∑ nⱼ ∈ Set.Icc (I j).1 (I j).2, (nⱼ⁻¹ : ℚ)) = n } := by
  sorry

/--
This is still open even if $|I_2| = 1$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_288.variants.i2_card_eq_1 : answer(sorry) ↔ Set.Finite { (I, n₂) : (ℕ+ × ℕ+) × ℕ+ |
    I.1 ≤ I.2 ∧ ∃ n : ℕ+, ∑ n₁ ∈ Set.Icc I.1 I.2, (n₁⁻¹ : ℚ) + (n₂⁻¹ : ℚ) = n } := by
  sorry

/--
It is perhaps true with two intervals replaced by any $k$ intervals.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_288.variants.k_intervals : answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ k, Set.Finite { I : Fin k → ℕ+ × ℕ+ |
    ∀ j, (I j).1 ≤ (I j).2 ∧
      ∃ n : ℕ+, (∑ j : Fin k, ∑ nⱼ ∈ Set.Icc (I j).1 (I j).2, (nⱼ⁻¹ : ℚ)) = n } := by
  sorry

/--
Is it true for any $k > 2$ that only finitely many $k$ intervals satisfy this condition?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_288.variants.exists_k_gt_2 : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∃ k > 2, Set.Finite { I : Fin k → ℕ+ × ℕ+ |
      ∀ j, (I j).1 ≤ (I j).2 ∧
        ∃ n : ℕ+, (∑ j : Fin k, ∑ nⱼ ∈ Set.Icc (I j).1 (I j).2, (nⱼ⁻¹ : ℚ)) = n } := by
  sorry

end Erdos288

reformulations.difference: Lean includes k = 0 and places the global integer-sum existential inside `∀ j`, alongside the nonemptiness condition for interval j. It also uses a positive-natural integer witness rather than a natural-number witness.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For k > 0, the global sum condition B is independent of j, so `∀ j, A j ∧ B` is equivalent to `(∀ j, A j) ∧ B`. Every permitted interval is nonempty and has positive rational reciprocal sum, so the total is positive and a natural-number witness is automatically positive. At k = 0, the tuple type `Fin 0 → ℕ+ × ℕ+` is a singleton; its solution set is therefore finite regardless of the vacuous predicate. Thus the additional zero case imposes no restriction. The full equivalence with finiteness of the naturally valued solution sets for every positive k was proved in the scratch file.

sources_consulted: P. Erdős and R. L. Graham, Old and New Problems and Results in Combinatorial Number Theory (1980), Chapter 4, especially printed p. 34: https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~ronspubs/80_11_number_theory.pdf
https://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/Erdos.html (bibliographic entries for the Erdős–Graham works)
review.notes:
Checked all four declarations. The final `exists_k_gt_2` declaration is an explicitly named weaker existence variant, separate from the universal k-interval conjecture. No status discrepancy was found in the accessible sources: the archived problem page and the currently retrieved independent database record the problem as open.

Live erdosproblems.com requests were blocked by Cloudflare, so the source comparison used archived pages and the original Erdős–Graham monograph. Lean experiments in /workspace/review/scratch.lean compiled successfully. They confirmed rational inversion, positive nonempty interval sums, the harmless k = 0 case, and quantifier equivalences. In particular, the singleton variant's `+ (n₂⁻¹ : ℚ)` is outside the summation by Mathlib's notation precedence; this was verified by definitional equality and by evaluating the source's example [3,6] together with {20}.
